newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia's energy industry urges electricity exports.
newsitem.headline: Serbia's energy industry urges electricity exports.

text.p: Serbia's power company Elektroprivreda Srbije (EPS) must be allowed to export more electricity to secure funds for rehaul of power plants and repayment of its debts, industry sources said.

"EPS must export in order to repay neighbouring countries for electricity and overhaul and revitalise its installations," Serbian Chamber of Commerce Energy Committee secretary Radoje Zecevic told a committee meeting Wednesday afternoon.
Last year, Serbia imported 3.9 billion KWh of electricity from neighbouring countries to tide it through the winter heating season, and exported 1.85 billion KWh.
EPS's problems are piling up, primarily inability to recover claims from consumers amounting to 1.87 billion dinars, and lack of funds to repay matured debts of 1.7 billion dinars.
"Now claims exceed the debt, which was not the case before," Zecevic said.
As much as 70 percent of EPS's claims are from the household sector, while in previous years industry accounted for the bulk of the debt to EPS.
Industry experts see exports as a means to secure funds for overhauls of thermal and hydro-electric power plants, some of which have been working for more than two decades.

"Expenses are huge and we cannot recover our claims. My firm has been blocked 14 months non-stop. Without exports I cannot see where we will get the money for overhauls," said Milos Mandic of the Bajina Basta hydro-electric plant.
Mandic suggested changing the structure of heating fuel consumption in favour of other fuels to free quantifies of electricity for export.
Serbian chamber of commerce officials said EPS's demands to raise the price of electricity would not resolve the problem and would only multiply claims from non-paying debtors.
A price hike would be a blow to the impoverished population in a country where the average monthly wage in March was barely over $100, and would ignite inflation.
Without an overhaul of power plants and repayment of debts, the energy sector would not be able to support economic development and recovery, industry sources said.
This year alone, around three billion dinars needed to be invested in overhaul and basic equipment.
"We must invest $400-600 million per year until the year 2000 to be able to revitalise the very large and very valuable system," Zecevic said.
EPS development strategy envisages investments of $2.60 billion by the year 2000 but the question is where the cash-strapped economy will secure such funds.

"We already do not have funds to cover the investment plans for this year. We cannot count on other sources and will have to rely more on local sources of funds," Ljubo Macic of EPS development office said.
Serbia plans to raise 1997 production of electricity by six percent, coal by 7-13 (depending on type), crude oil by 1.2 and natural gas 1.8 percent compared to 1996.
Electricity output in 1996 was 33,159 GWh, of which 13,183 GWh was hydroelectric, and 19,969 GWh thermal power, a drop of 1.3 percent on 1995.
In the first two months of 1997, Serbia produced 6,494 GWh of electricity, or 11.4 percent below plan.

"We must secure enough energy for the economy to function. If economic activity were to pick up abruptly, we would not have enough energy to meet its needs," said Stanisa Paunovic, president of the Chamber's Energy Committee.
